newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Senior officials to discuss fish cut plans.
newsitem.headline: Senior officials to discuss fish cut plans.

text.p: Senior fisheries officials from European Union capitals are due to meet on Thursday to discuss controversial plans for sharp fishing cuts over the next three years to the end of 1999.

EU diplomats said that the Dutch EU Presidency will present a new document highlighting problem areas following discussion last week by a fisheries working group of a European Commission paper revising its new three-pronged approach to the 4th Multiannual Guidance Programme.
Under the new approach, member states would be given responsibility for drawing up national fleet reduction programmes.
The Commission would play a bigger role in ensuring that the programmes were effectively implemented and permanent.
The Commission would also closely control renewal of the fishing fleet to prevent any increase in surplus capacity.
But member states were sceptical and found it difficult to understand how the new ideas would work in practice.
"The text needs to be clarified...there are still a lot of questions," said one diplomat.
The main areas of disagreement concern:
- Fishing reduction rates: Proposed cuts of 30 percent and 20 percent for endangered and overfished stocks are considered too high by most member states.
- Stocks: some countries believe that stocks data justifying sharp fishing cuts are now outdated.

- Method of achieving fishing reduction targets: Either by reduction in fishing capacity or fishing effort or a combination of both. There was also disagreement over whether fishing effort should be calculated by species in a geographic area or by type of fishing vessel.
Some countries want tonnage increases due to safety improvements to be excluded when calculating fleet capacity reductions.

- Fleet renewal: major fishing nations oppose plans which they say would give the Commission control over the construction of new fishing vessels. A formula would be fixed for each type of new vessel under which a certain number of old vessels must be laid up depending on the type of boat and fishery.
"It's by no means clear how this will work or even where we are going," said another official.
